los.text: Describe the anatomy of the superior and inferior radio-ulnar joints
los.html:
JointTypeDetail
Superior radioulnarSynovial pivotRadial head turns in a ring of annular ligament + radial notch of ulna; shares the elbow capsule
Inferior radioulnarSynovial pivot
  • Ulnar head in the ulnar notch of the radius
  • Triangular fibrocartilage (TFCC) binds the two bones and keeps the ulna off the carpus
Interosseous membraneFibrous (syndesmosis)Fibres run down from radius to ulna, passing load from the radius (wrist) to the ulna (elbow)
MovementThe radius rotates around the ulna (axis through the radial and ulnar heads) in pronation and supination.
Pulled elbow(toddlers)Radial head slips out of the annular ligament after a sudden pull on the arm.

los.text: Recognise the movements of supination and pronation and identify the muscles involved whilst summarising their main attachments and nervous innervation
los.html:
MovementMuscleAttachmentsNerve
SupinationBiceps brachiiRadial tuberosityMusculocutaneous
SupinatorLateral epicondyle, supinator crest of ulna → wraps round proximal radiusDeep radial (PIN)
PronationPronator teresMedial epicondyle + coronoid → lateral mid-radiusMedian
Pronator quadratusDistal ulna → distal radius (front)Anterior interosseous (median)
  • Biceps is the strongest supinator, best with the elbow flexed (screwdriver action); supination is stronger than pronation.
  • Brachioradialis brings the forearm to mid-position from either extreme.

los.text: Describe and recognise movements at the wrist joint and identify the muscle groups responsible
los.html:
• Wrist (radiocarpal) joint: synovial ellipsoid: radius and TFCC with scaphoid, lunate and triquetrum (the ulna doesn't touch the carpus).
    • The midcarpal joint adds movement.
MovementMusclesNerve
FlexionFCR, FCU, palmaris longus (+ finger flexors)Median (FCR, PL), ulnar (FCU)
ExtensionECRL, ECRB, ECU (+ finger extensors)Radial
Radial deviation (abduction)FCR + ECRL/ECRBMedian + radial
Ulnar deviation (adduction)FCU + ECUUlnar + radial
  • Ulnar deviation has more range (the radial styloid reaches further down).
  • Synergy: wrist extensors fire during gripping so finger flexors stay at a strong length
    • radial palsy weakens grip for this reason.

los.text: Recognise the positions and functions of the retinacula of the wrist and the tendon sheaths of the wrist and hand, and relate them to carpal tunnel syndrome and the spread of infection in tendon sheaths
los.html:
Flexor retinaculumFrom pisiform and hook of hamate (medial) to scaphoid tubercle and trapezium (lateral); roof of the carpal tunnel.
Carpal tunnel contentsMedian nerve + 9 tendons (4 FDS, 4 FDP, FPL); FCR in its own split of the retinaculum.
Superficial to itUlnar nerve and artery (Guyon's canal), palmaris longus, palmar cutaneous branch of median (so palm sensation is spared in carpal tunnel syndrome).
Carpal tunnel syndrome
  • Tingling in the lateral 3½ digits (worse at night), thenar wasting, weak abductor pollicis brevis
  • Pregnancy, hypothyroidism, RA, diabetes, acromegaly
  • Phalen's and Tinel's tests
  • Treat by dividing the retinaculum.
Extensor compartmentTendons
1APL, EPB (de Quervain's tenosynovitis)
2ECRL, ECRB
3EPL (turns round Lister's tubercle)
4Extensor digitorum, extensor indicis
5Extensor digiti minimi
6ECU
Flexor sheaths
  • Ulnar bursa (common sheath for FDS and FDP) runs on into the little finger's sheath
  • Radial bursa (FPL) into the thumb's
  • Index, middle and ring sheaths are separate.
Infection
  • Flexor tenosynovitis (Kanavel signs: fusiform swelling, flexed finger, tenderness along the sheath, pain on passive extension).
  • Little finger or thumb infections can spread into the bursae (horseshoe abscess) and up into the forearm.

los.text: Describe the close relationships of the bones and joints of the forearm and wrist with other structures, e.g. blood vessels, nerves, ligaments, tendons and bursae, which may be injured in fracture and dislocation, and recognise the affects of such damage upon function
los.html:
InjuryStructure at riskEffect
Distal radius fracture (Colles: dorsal tilt, "dinner fork")Median nerve; EPL tendon later (Lister's tubercle); DRUJ/TFCCAcute carpal tunnel; can't extend thumb; painful rotation
Scaphoid fractureRetrograde blood supply (distal to proximal)Avascular necrosis of the proximal pole, non-union
Lunate dislocation (anterior)Median nerve in the carpal tunnelAcute carpal tunnel syndrome
Supracondylar fracture (child)Brachial artery, median/anterior interosseous nerveVolkmann's ischaemic contracture
Forearm shaft fracturesCompartments; Monteggia (ulna + radial head) risks the posterior interosseous nerveCompartment syndrome; wrist/finger drop
Hook of hamate fractureUlnar nerve and artery (Guyon's canal)Weak intrinsics, numb little finger
Wrist lacerationMedian nerve (between FCR and PL), ulnar nerve and artery, radial artery, tendonsLoss of function depends on what's cut

los.text: Describe the anatomical basis of the assessment of cutaneous sensation in the dermatomes of the upper limb and tendon jerk tests
los.html:
DermatomeArea
C4Cape over the top of the shoulder
C5Lateral arm (deltoid region)
C6Lateral forearm, thumb (and index)
C7Middle finger
C8Little finger, medial hand and forearm
T1Medial forearm and elbow
T2Axilla, upper medial arm
ReflexRootMyotomeRoot
BicepsC5–6Shoulder abductionC5
BrachioradialisC5–6Elbow flexion, wrist extensionC6
TricepsC7Elbow extension, wrist flexionC7
Finger flexionC8
Finger abductionT1
  • Use: a dermatomal pattern (e.g. numb thumb + weak elbow flexion + reduced biceps jerk = C6 root) differs from a peripheral nerve pattern.

los.text: Name and demonstrate the movements of the fingers and thumb
los.html:
Fingers
  • MCP joints (condyloid) flex, extend, abduct and adduct (around the middle finger's axis)
  • PIP and DIP joints (hinge) flex and extend.
Thumb CMC joint(saddle, trapezium–1st metacarpal)
  • Flexion/extension in the plane of the palm
  • Abduction/adduction at right angles to the palm
  • Opposition = flexion + abduction + medial rotation (pulp to pulp)
  • Reposition.
The thumb's planes are rotated 90° to the fingers' (the thumbnail faces sideways).

los.text: Identify the muscles and tendons involved in the movements of the fingers and thumb (differentiating between those in the forearm and those intrinsic to the hand) and name their attachments and nervous innervation
los.html:
Extrinsic (forearm)InsertsActionNerve
FDSMiddle phalanges (splits round FDP)Flexes PIPMedian
FDPDistal phalangesThe only DIP flexorMedian (AIN: index, middle) + ulnar (ring, little)
FPLThumb distal phalanxFlexes thumb IPAnterior interosseous
Extensor digitorumExtensor expansionsExtends MCPs (and IPs via the hood)Radial (PIN)
EPL / EPB / APLThumb distal phalanx / proximal phalanx / 1st metacarpal baseExtend IP / extend MCP / abduct thumbRadial (PIN)
Intrinsic (hand)ActionNerve
Thenar: APB, FPB, opponens pollicisThumb abduction, flexion, oppositionMedian (recurrent branch)
Adductor pollicisThumb adductionUlnar (deep)
Hypothenar: ADM, FDM, ODMLittle finger movementsUlnar
Lumbricals (from FDP tendons)Flex MCP, extend IPsLateral 2 median, medial 2 ulnar
Interossei: palmar (PAD, adduct) and dorsal (DAB, abduct)Finger ad/abduction; flex MCP, extend IPsUlnar (deep)
  • Bedside tests: FDS: hold the other fingers straight, flex the PIP. FDP: hold the PIP, flex the DIP.

los.text: Recognise the main types of grip (power, precision and hook) and the roles of the muscles and nerves involved in executing them, and describe how muscle groups work in synergy to facilitate action
los.html:
GripWhat happensKey musclesNerves
PowerObject clamped between flexed fingers and palm, thumb over the top; wrist extendedFDS, FDP, interossei, adductor pollicis, thenar and hypothenar; wrist extensors stabiliseMedian, ulnar (+ radial for the wrist)
Precision (pinch)Thumb pulp to finger pulpOpposition (opponens, APB, FPB), FPL, FDP, interossei; adductor pollicis for key pinchMedian (opposition), ulnar (fine control)
HookFingers flexed at IP joints, thumb not used (carrying a bag)FDS, FDPMedian, ulnar
  • Synergy: wrist extensors stop the finger flexors bending the wrist
    • antagonists co-contract to stabilise
    • thumb opposition balances thenar muscles with adductor pollicis.

los.text: Label a diagram of the muscles and tendons of the palm of the hand
los.html:
Layer (superficial → deep)Contents
1Skin, palmar aponeurosis (Dupuytren's contracture), palmaris brevis
2Superficial palmar arch, digital nerves (median and ulnar)
3FDS tendons, then FDP tendons with the lumbricals; FPL to the thumb
4Thenar (APB, FPB, then opponens) and hypothenar (ADM, FDM, ODM) muscles
5Deep palmar arch, deep branch of ulnar nerve, adductor pollicis
6Palmar and dorsal interossei, metacarpals
  • Fibrous flexor sheaths: annular (A1–A5) and cruciate pulleys; A2 and A4 stop bowstringing; A1 is where trigger finger catches.

los.text: Label a diagram of the muscles and tendons of the dorsal hand
los.html:
Tendons from the six compartments
  • APL and EPB (front of the snuffbox), EPL (back of the snuffbox)
  • ECRL and ECRB to bases of metacarpals 2 and 3
  • Extensor digitorum (four tendons linked by juncturae tendinum)
  • Extensor indicis (on the ulnar side of the index tendon)
  • Extensor digiti minimi
  • ECU to the base of the 5th metacarpal.
Extensor expansion (hood)Over the proximal phalanx; receives lumbricals and interossei; central slip → middle phalanx base, lateral bands → distal phalanx base.
InjuryStructureDeformity
Mallet fingerTerminal tendon at the DIPDrooping fingertip
BoutonnièreCentral slipPIP flexed, DIP hyperextended
Swan neckVolar plate / imbalancePIP hyperextended, DIP flexed
Dorsal interosseiThe first is visible in the first web space (wastes in ulnar palsy).
Also on the dorsumVenous network → cephalic (lateral) and basilic (medial) veins; superficial radial nerve; dorsal branch of the ulnar nerve.

los.text: Locate the radial artery and superficial branch of the radial nerve
los.html:
Radial artery
  • From the brachial at the neck of the radius
  • → under brachioradialis
  • → at the wrist lateral to the FCR tendon on the distal radius (radial pulse, ABG site)
  • → winds round the back through the anatomical snuffbox
  • → between the heads of the first dorsal interosseous
  • → forms the deep palmar arch.
Superficial radial nerve
  • Under brachioradialis (lateral to the artery)
  • → emerges between brachioradialis and ECRL ~7 cm above the wrist
  • → crosses the snuffbox
  • → skin of the lateral dorsum (1st web space).
  • Purely sensory: a tight watch strap or cast causes numbness without weakness.

los.text: Locate the ulnar artery and ulnar nerve
los.html:
Ulnar artery
  • The larger branch of the brachial
  • → deep to pronator teres and FDS
  • → meets the ulnar nerve (nerve on its medial side) under FCU
  • → at the wrist lateral to the FCU tendon and pisiform
  • → Guyon's canal (superficial to the flexor retinaculum)
  • → main source of the superficial palmar arch.
Ulnar nerve
  • Behind the medial epicondyle
  • → between the heads of FCU
  • → under FCU beside the artery
  • → dorsal cutaneous branch ~5 cm above the wrist (spared in a Guyon's canal lesion)
  • → Guyon's canal
  • → superficial (sensory, palmaris brevis) and deep branch (round the hook of hamate: hypothenar, interossei, medial lumbricals, adductor pollicis).

los.text: Identify the bones of the wrist and hand and their relative positions, identifying those that are commonly damaged and be able to predict functional impairment following such damage
los.html:
Carpals(proximal row lateral → medial)Scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform; distal row: trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate ("Some Lovers Try Positions That They Can't Handle").
Then5 metacarpals; 14 phalanges (thumb 2, each finger 3).
Commonly damagedMechanismProblem
Scaphoid (most common carpal fracture)Fall on outstretched hand; snuffbox tendernessEarly X-ray may miss it; avascular necrosis of the proximal pole, non-union, arthritis
LunateDislocates forwardsAcute carpal tunnel syndrome; Kienböck's AVN
Hook of hamateGolf, racquet sportsUlnar nerve palsy
5th metacarpal neck ("boxer's fracture")PunchingCheck rotation (fingers crossing on flexion)
Bennett's fractureBase of 1st metacarpal, into the jointUnstable (APL pulls the shaft); thumb function

los.text: Identify the key features of the carpal, metacarpal and phalangeal bones
los.html:
BoneKey features
ScaphoidBoat-shaped; tubercle (base of thenar eminence, retinaculum); fractures at the waist; floor of the snuffbox
LunateCrescent; articulates with the radius; most often dislocated carpal bone
TriquetrumPyramidal; the pisiform sits on it
PisiformPea-shaped sesamoid in the FCU tendon
TrapeziumSaddle facet for the 1st metacarpal; groove for FCR
TrapezoidSmall wedge; 2nd metacarpal
CapitateLargest, central; 3rd metacarpal; first to ossify
HamateHook for the retinaculum and Guyon's canal; 4th and 5th metacarpals
MetacarpalsBase, shaft, head (knuckles); 1st shortest and most mobile; 2nd longest; 3rd has a styloid process.
PhalangesBase, shaft, head; distal phalanx ends in a tuft for the pulp.
OssificationCapitate (~1 year) through to pisiform (~12 years): basis of hand X-ray bone age.

los.text: Draw a labelled diagram of the superficial and deep palmar arches describing the vascular supply of the hand and recognise major vessels in angiograms
los.html:
ArchMain sourcePositionBranches
Superficial palmarUlnar artery (+ radial superficial branch)Level with the distal border of the fully abducted thumb; under the palmar aponeurosis, over the flexor tendonsCommon → proper palmar digital arteries
Deep palmarRadial artery (+ deep ulnar branch)~1 cm proximal, on the metacarpal bases, under the flexor tendonsPalmar metacarpal arteries, perforators; princeps pollicis, radialis indicis
Allen's testPress on both arteries, let the hand blanch, release the ulnar: colour returning shows ulnar flow can supply the hand (before radial ABG, cannulation or harvest).
AngiogramsShow the arches; they are incomplete in some people.

los.text: Define the boundaries of the anatomical 'snuff box'
los.html:
BoundaryFormed by
Lateral (radial)Tendons of APL and EPB
Medial (ulnar)Tendon of EPL
ProximalRadial styloid
FloorScaphoid and trapezium
RoofSkin, start of the cephalic vein, superficial radial nerve
ContentsRadial artery crossing the floor; cephalic vein; superficial radial nerve.
ClinicalTenderness here after a fall = scaphoid fracture until proven otherwise.
